h: A country convicted for the first time: justice at last for the Rohingya
dek: In Scroll, genocide scholar Max Pensky writes that the international court's verdict holding Myanmar guilty of genocide is both a victory for the Rohingya and a new precedent for the Gaza case.
body: On 19 November, the International Court of Justice (ICJ) at The Hague ruled in The Gambia v. Myanmar that Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya Muslims. Max Pensky of Binghamton University sees it as a big win for the small African country that filed the case in 2019, but says its echo will reach far beyond the two countries.

The case concerns the 2017 'clearance operations' that Myanmar's army, the Tatmadaw, kept calling a counter-insurgency campaign. Hundreds of villages were burned, and there was rape, torture and killing. At least ten thousand people are believed to have been killed, and about 750,000 fled to Bangladesh. The court found that the pattern of the attacks and the targeted selection of victims could not be explained as counter-insurgency. They had only one reasonable meaning: the intent to wipe out the community.

The writer explains that this is a first in many ways. In the Bosnia case in 2007, the court held Serbia only to have failed to prevent the Srebrenica massacre. This time a country has been held responsible for committing genocide. Myanmar must run a full reparations programme, create conditions for people to return safely and with dignity, and restore the citizenship that a 1982 law took away, leaving the Rohingya stateless.

The most far-reaching point is that the court accepted The Gambia's argument that the duty under the Genocide Convention is shared by every member state, even one that has suffered no direct harm. According to Pensky, this gives direct strength to the South Africa v. Israel case, which alleges genocide in Gaza.

The ICJ has no machinery to enforce its ruling, so Myanmar cannot be forced to comply. Still, the writer says, the stigma of being the first 'genocidal state' opens the way to sanctions and arms embargoes. In an age of weakening international institutions, this is a rare victory for justice, above all for the Rohingya, who were chanting 'Thank you, Gambia' in the camps.
nazar: After this verdict, it is no longer easy to brush the Rohingya aside as 'infiltrators'. People whom the world's highest court has recognised as victims of genocide are being kept in India, from Jammu to Delhi, under the fear of detention, eviction and deportation. India signed the Genocide Convention in 1959, and this verdict is a reminder that the signature must carry some weight.

The second lesson is for Gaza. A small African country has shown that one can fight for justice without being powerful. The countries of the Global South that choose to stay silent, India among them, no longer even have the excuse that the law can do nothing.
sawal: Will India still call the Rohingya, victims of genocide, 'infiltrators'?
ref: Genocide Convention, 1948

The first major treaty of the UN General Assembly, which defines as genocide the killing and persecution carried out with intent to destroy a racial, religious or national group. India ratified it in 1959.
Erga omnes partes
A Latin term meaning 'towards all parties to the treaty'. Under it, any member state can go to court over genocide, even if it has suffered no direct harm.
ank: Fled to Bangladesh to save their lives
photo_note: Representative image: Kutupalong refugee camp, Bangladesh

h: The victims of genocide stand before us. Which side will India take?
dek: In The Wire, Supreme Court lawyer Tanima Kishore writes that after the ICJ verdict, India's debate on the Rohingya must move beyond infiltration and security.
body: On 19 November, the international court ruled that Myanmar's army committed genocide against the Rohingya in Rakhine in 2017. According to Tanima Kishore, a human rights lawyer and Advocate-on-Record in the Supreme Court, the verdict asks India to rethink its stand. For nearly ten years, talk about the Rohingya in India has revolved around infiltration, security and citizenship, and policy has been shaped the same way.

The writer says it is now recorded in international law that the Rohingya are victims of genocide, and every discussion of their future must start from there. The first article of the Genocide Convention places on states a duty not only to punish genocide but also to prevent it. In the 2007 Bosnia v. Serbia verdict, the court said that when a state knows, or should know, of a serious risk, it must act.

India accepted the convention in 1959. The writer agrees that the convention does not force India to grant citizenship or give up immigration control, and that security checks and the regulation of migration are legitimate. But there is a difference between handling ordinary migrants and the policy towards a community that a court has recognised as victims of genocide. Reports of Rohingya families in Jammu having their homes torn down after notices, and of the alleged deportation of 38 people without a hearing, must be seen in this light.

The verdict does not create new refugee obligations, but it strengthens the case against sending people back to a place of persecution. The writer reminds us that India has sheltered Tibetans, Sri Lankan Tamils and Afghans. Her conclusion is that genocide does not end at the border, and history will judge India by whether it chose exclusion or protection for the survivors.
nazar: In its statement on the verdict, India only 'noted' it and did not even use the word genocide. When a country that sheltered Tibetans and Tamils looks at the Rohingya through the lens of religion, it raises questions about the double standard in its asylum policy. Only a written refugee law can stop this arbitrariness.
sawal: If Tibetans and Tamils are refugees, why are the Rohingya infiltrators?
ref: Bosnia v. Serbia, 2007
The ICJ verdict that held Serbia to have failed to prevent the Srebrenica genocide. It established that states must take steps to prevent genocide once they know of the risk.
Non-refoulement
The principle of international law that a refugee cannot be sent back to a country where their life or freedom is in danger.

h: The Reykjavik dream in Shenzhen: can nuclear weapons be ended?
dek: In Al Jazeera, historians Peter Kuznick and Ivana Nikolić Hughes write that if Trump, Putin and Xi wish, they can open a path to ridding the world of nuclear weapons in twelve years.
body: Some are calling the possible meeting of Trump, Putin and Xi in Shenzhen a 'second Yalta'. The writers want to see it become a 'second Reykjavik'. In 1986, in Iceland's capital, Reagan offered to abolish ballistic missiles, Gorbachev proposed abolishing all nuclear weapons, and Reagan even agreed. The deal broke down only because Reagan would not agree to confine testing of his 'Star Wars' missile defence programme to the laboratory for ten years.

The obstacles are many. After defeat in the midterm elections, Trump has made Stephen Miller his chief of staff. A big basis of Putin's power is Russia's vast nuclear arsenal. And Xi says China will not come to the table unless the large arsenals shrink, even as China expands its own. The writers believe Putin's nuclear threats have also damaged the credibility of such promises.

Still, there are signs of hope. Trump has for years called nuclear weapons the greatest danger and, after his defeat, may be looking for a legacy. Putin said in 2017 that disarmament was possible, and Xi said that same year that these weapons should be banned and destroyed.

The writers propose three stages of four years each. First, the US and Russia cut their more than five thousand weapons each down to about 600, on par with China, China halts its expansion, and the wars in Iran and Ukraine end. Then all nine nuclear states negotiate and join the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons. Finally, complete elimination with verification, by the hundredth anniversary of Hiroshima and Nagasaki.
nazar: The article does not name India and Pakistan, but both are among the 'nine nuclear states', and South Asia is the world's most dangerous nuclear neighbourhood. India has boycotted the Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons. In a country where crores of people are still far from a good school or hospital, asking for an account of spending on the bomb is also patriotism.
sawal: What will India bring to the table of the nine nuclear states?
ref: Reykjavik summit, 1986
The meeting of Reagan and Gorbachev in Iceland, where they nearly agreed to abolish all nuclear weapons. It broke down over differences on the missile defence programme.
Treaty on the Prohibition of Nuclear Weapons
A treaty adopted at the UN in 2017 that makes nuclear weapons completely illegal. No nuclear state, India included, has joined it.

h: Looser rules for animal testing put human health at stake
dek: In Newslaundry, Ambika Shukla writes that the new draft rules on animal experiments will not only add to cruelty against animals but also damage the credibility of India's medicines and science.
body: The writer's argument is simple: an experiment without proper oversight produces data you cannot trust, and a medicine built on weak data finally gambles with human lives. So the 2026 draft rules on animal experiments are not just an issue for animal lovers or scientists, but for everyone who takes a medicine made in India.

She recalls that when the oversight committee set up under the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960, became active around 2000, it found gross negligence in laboratories: 27 monkeys kept for years in bird cages, and absurd experiments that drowned rats again and again. After this came good laboratory practices, tighter oversight and less use of animals in cosmetic testing, and according to the writer, this is what made India a major producer of medicines and vaccines.

Under the new draft, instead of animals bred for research, animals brought from the streets, shelters or markets could be used, with no record of their health or breed. Experiments could also be done outside controlled laboratories, in mobile set-ups. Oversight would move from the centre to the institutions' own ethics committees, even though those same institutions have interests of money and reputation at stake.

The details hurt even more: notice will be given before inspections, starvation will count as a 'mild' procedure and inducing tumours as 'moderate', the conditions for anaesthesia will be relaxed, there will be blanket approvals of up to five years for teaching, and the same animal can be used for repeated experiments. After the deadline for comments ended on 5 November, opinions are now being sought only from medical colleges, which leads the writer to ask whether the outcome is already decided.

The world is moving towards alternatives such as human cells, organoids and computer models. The writer wants India to invest in these too, to make binding the three principles of replace, reduce and refine, and to withdraw the present draft, because animals cannot object to their condition, and their silence is not consent.
nazar: The bill for loose oversight is finally paid by the weakest person: the patient who depends on the cheapest medicine in a government hospital, and the worker whose complaint no one hears. When only the institutions that gain from the relaxations are invited to the rule-making table, this is not reform but convenience for business.
sawal: By whose measure is starvation a 'mild' procedure?
ref: CPCSEA
The central committee set up to control and supervise the use of animals in experiments. Under the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals Act, 1960, it registers and inspects laboratories.
The Three Rs
Three ethical principles of animal testing: use another method in place of animals wherever possible, use as few animals as possible, and cause as little suffering as possible.

h: Echoes of the 1930s: Ram Puniyani's warning
dek: In Countercurrents, Ram Puniyani writes that from the intensive revision of voter rolls to the capture of institutions, today's crisis is rooted in an ideology inspired by European fascism.
body: At the closing session of India Summit 2026, Rahul Gandhi said fascist rule in the country began in 2014. Ram Puniyani offers arguments in support. His first piece of evidence is the Special Intensive Revision of the voter rolls, against which civil society groups across the country have come out, because it could strip lakhs of people of their right to vote. The writer alleges that peaceful protesters were beaten.

He cites figures from the V-Dem Institute: India ranks 106th of 179 countries on the electoral democracy index, and its score is the lowest since the Emergency. Pointing to Assam's NRC, he says that among the roughly two million people who could not produce citizenship papers, a large number were Hindus, which means the 'infiltrators' story does not stand on facts.

Then he turns to history. According to the writer, B.S. Moonje of the Hindu Mahasabha met Mussolini in Italy after the Round Table Conference and came back impressed by its youth organisation. Golwalkar, the second sarsanghchalak (chief) of the RSS, in his 1938 book held up Nazi Germany's anti-Jewish 'purification' as a lesson for Hindustan, and named Muslims, Christians and Communists as internal enemies.

Puniyani recalls sociologist Ashis Nandy, who years ago, after a conversation with Narendra Modi, called fascism not an insult but a diagnosis. According to the writer, Indian fascism differs from Germany's in that religious identity, not race, is the tool here: through the Ram temple, the cow and 'love jihad', while the coffers of big corporations fill up alongside.

He believes the values of the Constitution and the freedom struggle are in grave danger, and that the intensive revision is the biggest danger because it targets exactly those voters who might go against those in power. Yet his conclusion is hopeful: with a joint effort, democracy can be restored.
nazar: Every drive that demands papers hits first those who have the fewest papers: migrant workers, Adivasis (indigenous people), Dalits, poor women and Muslims. Many of Puniyani's claims invite debate, but his question is fair: when deleting names from the voter list becomes a political tool, what is left of democracy?
sawal: Who will speak for the Hindus in Assam who could not show papers?
ref: V-Dem Institute

A research institute at the University of Gothenburg in Sweden that measures the state of democracy in countries around the world every year. It has placed India in the category of 'electoral autocracy'.
Special Intensive Revision (SIR)
The Election Commission's fresh check of the voter rolls, in which people are asked for documents. Critics allege it is pushing large numbers of poor and marginalised people off the rolls.

h: New provinces in Pakistan: a debate in the papers, not in Parliament
dek: A Dawn editorial says the PPP and PML-N tussle over creating new provinces is being fought in the media, when a decision to redraw the map can only be made by consensus in Parliament and the provincial assemblies.
body: On the question of creating new provinces in Pakistan, the two big partners in the ruling coalition, the PPP and the PML-N, are each invoking democracy in their own way, and according to Dawn, both are hardening their positions.

At the Karachi Press Club, Bilawal Bhutto Zardari said that if provinces were divided by force, there could be bloodshed. He recalled that in Pakistan's history referendums have often been held to rubber-stamp undemocratic acts, and also said that neither the prime minister nor any minister had spoken to him or the president on the issue. He wants a 'political reset' in which the mandate of the opposition, especially the PTI, is accepted.

On the other side, PML-N ministers are calling a nationwide referendum the fairest route, even though disputes over the last general election are still unresolved. The interior, defence and information ministers are speaking loudly on TV and in statements, but the prime minister is silent, and the president's silence also seems odd. The editorial guesses that the top leaders may be testing the public mood through Bilawal and second-rung ministers.

Dawn's view is that this is not an issue to be put off. Changing provincial borders means reshaping almost every government department, and it cannot be done by decree. Under the Constitution, changing a province's borders needs a two-thirds majority in that province's assembly. So instead of ultimatums and demands for a referendum, the matter should be taken to Parliament and the provincial assemblies to build consensus.
nazar: India saw in Jammu and Kashmir in 2019 that when the map is changed from above and the elected assembly is not even asked, the wound to trust lasts a long time. Dawn's point applies on both sides of the border: smaller units can give a voice to neglected regions, but only when the people there are asked. Otherwise it is a division of power, not of the people's say.
sawal: Will the assembly of the province to be divided be asked?
ref: Referendums in Pakistan
In Pakistan, Zia-ul-Haq in 1984 and Pervez Musharraf in 2002 held referendums to legitimise their presidencies, and both were widely seen as rigged.
PPP and PML-N
The Pakistan Peoples Party (the Bhutto family's party, strong in Sindh) and the Pakistan Muslim League-Nawaz (the Sharif family's party, strong in Punjab), now partners in the ruling coalition.

h: Gaza: Israel's own figures, and the West's brazenness
dek: In Middle East Eye, Jonathan Cook writes that aid to Gaza is being blocked even after the ceasefire, and that governments like Britain's and the big media have made genocide denial normal.
body: Jonathan Cook begins with the Genocide Convention's definition, under which deliberately inflicting on a group conditions of life meant to destroy it is also genocide. He says that this time the evidence is Israel's own figures, which the newspaper Haaretz obtained through a freedom of information request.

In the ceasefire, Israel promised to let in 18,200 trucks a month, about 600 a day. In March only 4,779 arrived, even September, the best month, fell 30 per cent short of the promise, and last month barely a third of the promised number got through. Over eight months the shortfall is more than 74,000 trucks. According to the writer, only 3 per cent of farmland remains usable, fishing is banned, and in the winter storms about 40,000 tents were flooded, while 150,000 tents are stuck outside the border.

Since the ceasefire, more than 1,600 Palestinians have been killed, more than 21,000 patients cannot leave for treatment, and Nasser Hospital was attacked again, killing six people, including a surgeon and a 13-year-old patient. Cook alleges this did not even make the news.

His real target is Britain. The government is washing its hands by sanctioning one Israeli group that blocks aid and some settlement-building companies, while, citing a Channel 4 investigation, he writes that arms export licences to Israel have more than tripled since 2024. He lists what Britain could do: stop the arms deals and about six billion pounds of trade, and join South Africa's case at the international court.

On the media, he cites a study showing that BBC presenters interrupted pro-Palestinian guests 252 times and pro-Israel guests only 15 times. According to the writer, genocide denial has now become respectable, and anyone who challenges it is called antisemitic or a supporter of terror.
nazar: This is a mirror for India: we too buy and sell weapons with Israel, and here too people who hold up placards for Palestine face cases. In a world where the hunger of an oppressed people is measured in a count of trucks and governments still stay silent, every weak community should understand that the protection of international law does not come on its own.
sawal: Who will ask where the 74,000 trucks were stopped?
ref: Genocide Convention, 1948
The UN treaty that makes it a crime to commit acts with intent to destroy, in whole or in part, a national, racial or religious group. India accepted it in 1959.
Yellow Line
The line drawn in Gaza after the ceasefire, on one side of which the Israeli army is deployed. According to the writer, Israel uses it to occupy about 70 per cent of Gaza.

h: Thiruparankundram: a lamp near the dargah this year, but no precedent
dek: The Supreme Court stayed the Madras High Court's ruling but gave one-time permission to light the Karthigai Deepam on the stone pillar on 24 November.
body: On Thiruparankundram hill in Madurai, about fifty metres from the Sikandar Badshah dargah (shrine), stands a stone pillar being called the Deepathoon. Some people had asked the High Court that the Karthigai Deepam lamp be lit right there. Justice G.R. Swaminathan granted the plea last December, and in January a division bench upheld it.

On Friday, a bench of Justice Aravind Kumar and Justice Vipul Pancholi stayed the High Court's ruling, but allowed the lamp to be lit once on 24 November. Only people chosen by the temple administration and government officials may go there, and the public will not be allowed. The court made clear that this will not be treated as proof of any tradition or as a claim for future years.

The Tamil Nadu government argued that there is no tradition of lighting a lamp there, and that according to the Agamas (temple scriptures) the lamp is lit near the Uchi Pillaiyar temple. The dargah's side said the judge inspected the site without informing the dargah, that a claim to a new tradition must be proved through a civil suit, not a writ petition, and that under a 1923 ruling the whole hill belongs to the dargah.
The petitioners said the pillar is not on the dargah's peak but on the neighbouring hill.
nazar: Even a one-time permission is a beginning, and the history of such disputes shows that 'only this year' often becomes next year's demand. On a hill where Jain caves, a temple and a dargah have stood together for centuries, the court must stop new claims from being laid in the name of tradition.
sawal: How will a distance of fifty metres protect centuries of sharing?
ref: Deepathoon
The stone pillar on which the right to light a lamp is claimed. The district administration has maintained it is a survey stone from the British era.
Karthigai Deepam
A festival of lamps celebrated in the Tamil month of Karthigai, when a large lamp is lit on hilltops.

h: Acquitted, but a bail order still follows him on Google
dek: The Delhi High Court said a plea to remove an old order in an Assam case must go to the Gauhati High Court, and said nothing on the question of privacy.
body: In September 2019, an FIR was filed in Assam against a man under sections including rape and marriage by deceit, and he was arrested the next day. The Gauhati High Court granted him bail that same month. Later the chargesheet came only under Section 498A, for dowry harassment, and in January 2021 the trial court acquitted him, finding the charge baseless. No one challenged this verdict.

Even so, typing his name into Google brings up that old bail order. Citing the harm to his reputation, he asked the Delhi High Court to have the order removed from name searches on Google and on sites like Indian Kanoon.

Justice Swarana Kanta Sharma dismissed the plea. The court said it was not enough that the petitioner lives in Delhi or that the order appears on the internet in Delhi. The order is from the Gauhati High Court and the whole case was heard in Assam, so that is the right forum.

The court said that if merely appearing online were enough to create jurisdiction, every High Court would start hearing cases about other courts' orders, opening the door to choosing a convenient court. The court gave no opinion on privacy or the 'right to be forgotten'.
nazar: In law, acquittal means complete freedom, but on the internet the shadow of the charge stays. Running between courts in two cities is not hard for a rich man, but for the poor, Muslims or Dalits who are trapped in false cases, this shadow can take away even jobs and relationships. A clear law on the right to be forgotten is needed.
sawal: Why should an old charge keep showing on Google after acquittal?
ref: Right to be forgotten
A person's claim that old information about them, no longer relevant, be removed from internet searches.
Article 226(2)
A High Court can issue orders in cases where the cause arose wholly or partly within its territory.

h: Talk of moving away from fossil fuels vanishes from the COP31 draft
dek: In the new draft at the Antalya climate summit, the electrification target survives, but the move away from oil and coal and the figure for adaptation money have been removed.
body: The new main draft of COP31, the climate summit under way in Antalya, Turkey, came out on 19 November. The 144-paragraph draft of 16 November has been replaced by a nine-page text, and every mention of transitioning away from fossil fuels has been taken out. There is also no mention of the promise made at COP28 in Dubai or of the roadmap drawn up under Brazil's presidency.
The earlier draft had a target of 120 billion dollars a year for adaptation by 2035. The new text has no amount and no baseline, only a proposal to discuss tripling adaptation finance by 2035.

What remains in the draft is the '35 by 35' target, that is, raising electricity's share of the world's total energy use to 35 per cent by 2035. Earlier it was clearly labelled voluntary; now that word has been dropped. The European Union supports it, while the Like-Minded Developing Countries group, which includes India, China, Egypt and Saudi Arabia, opposes putting it in the main decision.
Avantika Goswami of CSE called the text a haphazard heap of targets. Panama has warned that if conditions such as a curb on oil production are not accepted, it will object at the final meeting.
nazar: By erasing the move away from oil and coal and dropping the money figure, rich countries are once again shifting the burden onto the poor. The fishers on India's coasts, the farmers of its dry regions and the workers living in city settlements are the very people who need adaptation money first, and they are the furthest from the table.
sawal: Where did the figure of 120 billion dollars go in three days?
ref: Cover decision
The main political document of a climate summit, which sets its direction and its big commitments.
Adaptation finance
Money given to poor countries to cope with impacts such as floods, drought and heat.

h: Siraj dropped, and an MP says his name is the reason
dek: Imran Masood's allegation over leaving Mohammed Siraj out of the first Test against New Zealand has set off a political debate.
body: Fast bowler Mohammed Siraj did not find a place in India's playing eleven for the first Test against New Zealand. Several former players also questioned the team management's decision and said an experienced bowler who performs well under pressure had been ignored.
On 20 November, Congress MP from Saharanpur Imran Masood alleged that Siraj was left out because of his religion. He said that looking at Siraj's name and his performance, no other reason made sense.

Union minister Kiren Rijiju said no one in the country faces discrimination on the basis of religion and that selection is on merit. BJP spokespersons accused Masood of dividing society and said players play for the country, not for any community.

NCP (Sharad Pawar) spokesperson Naseem Siddiqui backed Masood and said Muslims face discrimination in the civil services, sports, the arts and academia. The report records no reason for the selection from the team management.
nazar: It is hard to prove that a single selection is directly tied to religion, and such allegations can also weaken the real question. But this debate comes up because Muslim players have been trolled again and again. If the reasons for selection were explained openly, there would be less room for suspicion.
sawal: Why don't the selectors themselves explain why Siraj was left out?
ref: Playing eleven
The eleven players who actually take the field in a match, chosen from the larger touring squad.
Imran Masood
Congress Lok Sabha MP from Saharanpur, who has been in controversies over his remarks before.

h: Two children drowned in an open sewer; compensation sixteen years later
dek: The Delhi High Court held the DDA and the Jal Board negligent for the deaths in a Pitampura park in 2010.
body: In April 2010, while playing in a public park in Delhi's Pitampura, two children, eleven-and-a-half-year-old Robiyal and Arjun, aged twelve and three quarters, fell into an open sewer and died. Their parents went to the High Court in 2016, accusing the agencies that ran the park and the sewer of negligence.

At the hearing, the DDA said that although the park was its own, the sewer work was being done by the Delhi Jal Board, so the responsibility was not its. The Jal Board said there were walls four to five feet high around the sewer, so precautions were complete. The police report, for its part, had blamed the children themselves for climbing over the wall.

Justice Jasmeet Singh rejected all these arguments. The court said that merely putting up a wall is no proof of safety, and that those who run a park owe greater care to children, because children cannot sense danger the way adults can. A quarrel between two agencies cannot be a reason to hold back compensation.

The court held both agencies jointly liable and ordered them to pay each family Rs 11.01 lakh, with 9 per cent annual interest from the date the petition was filed. Each family will also get Rs 1 lakh separately for the costs of the case.
nazar: Open sewers and pits are fewer in rich neighbourhoods and more common in workers' settlements and the parks around them, and the children who fall into them also often come from poor homes. This verdict, coming sixteen years later, is welcome, but its real test will be when the city's other open manholes are covered.
sawal: When, in sixteen years, was that Pitampura sewer covered?
ref: Res ipsa loquitur
A Latin legal principle meaning 'the thing speaks for itself'. When the circumstances themselves show negligence, the burden of proving it is reduced.
Joint and several liability
Both agencies are responsible for paying the full amount, together and separately; the family can recover it from either.

h: Fear of NRC through Census 2027 reaches the United Nations
dek: The South Asia Justice Campaign said the census questions, a demography committee and private enumerators together could target Muslims.
body: In a submission sent on 14 November to the UN human rights office, the South Asia Justice Campaign, a platform of civil society groups, has warned that the first census since 2011 could lay the ground for a nationwide NRC (National Register of Citizens). According to the group, the questionnaire notified on 14 August 2026 asks for identity card numbers, parents' names, religion, place of birth, mobile number, voter ID and Aadhaar number. Eight of the 40 questions resemble the 2020 NPR form, which the Home Ministry has called the first step towards the NRC.

The second concern is the high-level committee on demographic change set up by the Home Ministry on 26 May 2026, chaired by a retired Supreme Court judge. The group says the committee's terms of reference already assume that illegal infiltration is the cause of population change, and that inviting information from the public opens the way to fabricated complaints.
On 16 October, the census rules were changed to allow private individuals to serve as enumerators too. According to the submission, this could let people with political motives into the count.

The group pointed to Assam, where about 19 lakh people were left out of the final NRC in 2019, yet even after seven years the list has not been notified and people have not received rejection slips to file appeals. Linking all this with the SIR, it has warned of the danger of statelessness.
nazar: A census is a necessary count, but when its questions look like a citizenship check and senior leaders of the government keep calling Muslims 'infiltrators', the fear is not without reason. In Assam, lakhs of people have been left in limbo for seven years. The government should give a clear written assurance that census data will not be used to decide citizenship.
sawal: Why does the census need to ask where one's parents were born?
ref: NPR
National Population Register. A register of everyone living in the country, which the government has called the first link in the citizenship register.
UN Special Procedures
Independent UN experts who hear complaints about the human rights situation in a country and ask governments for answers.

h: In Tinsukia, people take to the streets against big dams
dek: A sit-in near the district deputy commissioner's office and a march through the town demanded a halt to mega hydropower projects in the Northeast, including Siang Upper.
body: In Tinsukia, Assam, on Friday, 20 November, hundreds of people gathered to oppose the 11,200 MW Siang Upper Multipurpose Project proposed in Arunachal Pradesh. The People's Forum Against Big Dams held a sit-in near the district deputy commissioner's office and marched through the town's main roads. It was the forum's first such protest in Tinsukia, and representatives of organisations from Arunachal also took part.

A memorandum sent to the Prime Minister through the deputy commissioner demands that all running and proposed mega hydropower projects in the Northeast be stopped at once. It calls for putting on hold the 278-metre-high Dibang dam, Siang Upper and the Demwe project proposed on the Lohit river. The forum has also asked the government to apply diplomatic pressure to stop China's 60,000 MW project on the Yarlung Tsangpo in Tibet.

The protesters argue that the region is fragile, prone to earthquakes, heavy rain and landslides. The Siang, Dibang and Lohit together form the Brahmaputra, so a big change in their flow will affect farming, fisheries and biodiversity in lower Assam. They cited the troubles of the Lower Subansiri project as a warning. Rahul Chhetri, an activist from Margherita, said the protest is not against development, but against development whose price is paid with people's lives and livelihoods.
nazar: The Adivasi (indigenous) communities of the Siang valley have long voiced fears of displacement and of their ancestral land going under water. Now voices rising downstream in Assam too show that the whole Brahmaputra basin is questioning a policy that treats the river only as a tool for power and for rivalry with China. Pushing aside local consent in the name of strategic need could backfire.
sawal: Who will ask the people on the lower banks of the Brahmaputra?
ref: Siang Upper Multipurpose Project
A proposed 11,200 MW hydropower and water storage scheme on the Siang river in Arunachal Pradesh. The government presents it as an answer to China's dam in Tibet.
ask: Stop all mega hydropower projects in the Northeast at once

h: Villagers detained before public hearing in Veerlapalem, Nalgonda
dek: Police allegedly picked up villagers and ward members opposing a distillery from their homes at dawn, so that they could not speak at the hearing.
body: An environmental public hearing was due in Veerlapalem village of Nalgonda district, Telangana, on a distillery proposed by Soham Agro Industries. It is alleged that before it began, at around six in the morning, Vadapally police entered homes and detained several villagers and elected representatives. Those picked up are said to include Ninavat Sipai and ward members Allam Nagaraju, Gunja Ramaiah, Angothu Balu, Rupavat Saidu and Ramavat Vinod.

For a long time their families did not know where they had been taken. Activists of the Human Rights Forum and Jana Vignana Vedika condemned the action. Kanneganti Ravi and K. Ravichander, co-convenors of the Telangana People's Joint Action Committee, demanded that everyone be released at once and allowed to take part in the hearing.

The company wants to set up a grain-based distillery worth Rs 750 crore on 108 acres, which would produce 400 kilolitres of ethanol and 200 kilolitres of extra neutral alcohol a day. It would also have a 15 megawatt power plant. Farmers fear falling groundwater, pollution and the ruin of fertile farmland. They say the environmental impact assessment plays down the dangers. Before the hearing, they had also gone to the Telangana High Court and the National Green Tribunal.
nazar: The whole point of a public hearing is that the people a project will affect can speak freely. If those who oppose it are picked up before the hearing, what remains is a paper formality. A policy that promotes ethanol as a green fuel should not run at the cost of the water of farming villages.
sawal: Whose hearing is a public hearing held without the people who oppose the project?
ref: Environmental public hearing
A legal process that records the views of affected people before a large industrial project gets environmental clearance. Its proceedings are placed before the committee that grants the clearance.
ask: Release those detained and let them speak at the public hearing

h: Delhi Police affidavit does not match what journalists went through
dek: Police told the Supreme Court that journalists were held by mistake and let go once identified, but the journalists who were detained tell a different story.
body: The Network of Women in Media, the Free Speech Collective, the Delhi Union of Journalists and the Kerala Union of Working Journalists have petitioned the Supreme Court over the detention of journalists during protests in Delhi in October against the SIR and the Chief Election Commissioner. In reply, Delhi Police filed an affidavit saying the journalists were either mistaken for protesters or moved while the crowd was being cleared, and were released as soon as their identity was confirmed.

About Ryan Thomas of The Caravan, the police say he was only moved from the spot. Thomas alleges he was beaten in a bus and then in a jeep. Ayush Tiwari of Scroll was in a bus for about an hour and a half and got out only when the bus caught fire. Journalists from Newslaundry and The Quint were held for three to five hours, even though the court had said on 11 October that journalists' work must not be obstructed.

The police call claims of seized equipment false, but journalists of The Mic Report got their camera back three or four days later, and Vinay Gupta of No Noise Stories got his camera back with a broken lens. No one received a seizure memo. The police closed the complaints of four women, saying no evidence was found.
nazar: The gap between the affidavit and the journalists' accounts is now before the court. If the police are free to decide who is a journalist and who is not, the first voices to be silenced are those of small digital outlets, regional reporters and women journalists. Reporting a protest is as basic a right as protesting.
sawal: In which register is a camera taken without a seizure memo recorded?
ref: SIR
The Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls. Protests have been going on in Delhi since October over allegations that this Election Commission process is cutting names on a large scale.
place: RK Ashram Marg and Connaught Place, New Delhi
ask: Accountability for the detention and beating of journalists covering protests

h: Sit-in at Leh's NDS Park goes on even on polling day
dek: Amid panchayat and municipal elections, the Leh Apex Body is firm on its demand to postpone the 4 December hill council elections.
body: Ladakh votes on Saturday, 21 November, for panchayats and urban bodies. Of 192 panchayats, sarpanches in 55 have already been elected unopposed. Voting will take place in all 21 wards of the Leh Municipal Council, while four of Kargil's 17 wards were decided unopposed. In Hanle Po village of the new Changthang district, a booth has been set up for 89 voters at a height of about 15,000 feet.

Meanwhile, the Leh Apex Body has announced that its protest will continue on polling day too. A sit-in and hunger strike have been going on at Leh's NDS Park since the day after Sonam Wangchuk was put under house arrest on 11 November. The body wants the Ladakh Autonomous Hill Development Council elections due on 4 December to be postponed, because about a quarter of the population moves to warmer places in winter.

Chairman Chering Dorjay Lakruk said the body has no role in these elections, and that voters should choose independents or parties that stand with its demands. He fears that after the elections the Centre will push new faces in place of the traditional leadership. According to Lakruk, there has been an informal message that talks will be held after the elections, but no written invitation has come so far.
nazar: Ladakh's movement began with big demands like statehood and the Sixth Schedule. Now it has come down to the basic question of when, and in what conditions, votes are cast. When a large part of the population is away and the best known face of the movement is under house arrest, an election held then creates less trust and more doubt.
sawal: How will the quarter of Ladakhis who leave in winter cast their votes?
ref: Leh Apex Body
A joint platform of religious, social and political groups of Leh which, together with the Kargil Democratic Alliance, demands statehood and constitutional safeguards for Ladakh.
ask: Hold the hill council elections after winter

h: ASHA workers hold their ground outside the CMO office in Dehradun
dek: Ten days into the agitation there is agreement on the honorarium, but ASHAs will not back down on their demand for a pension and retirement package.
body: The agitation of ASHA workers in Uttarakhand grew stronger on its tenth day. On Friday, 20 November, about 150 ASHAs sat outside the office of the Chief Medical Officer, or CMO, in Dehradun. They raised slogans and warned that if their demands were not met, they would march to the Secretariat again.

The ASHAs have a seven-point charter of demands. They have already marched to the Secretariat. After a day-long sit-in, talks with officials led to agreement on raising the honorarium, but the workers are firm on a retirement package of five lakh rupees, a pension and their other demands. They say a rise in honorarium alone will not do.

The government had given a meeting time on 19 November, but the talks never took place. After that the ASHAs began a sit-in at the CMO office. They have now been given the date of 23 November. Shiva Dubey, president of the Uttarakhand ASHA Health Workers Union, said the sit-in will go on until all demands are met. Many workers, including Prabha Chaudhary, Meera Negi, Asha Bhatt, Sarojini and Rinki, took part.
nazar: ASHA workers are the backbone of care for mothers and children, vaccination and disease monitoring in villages, yet they are treated as volunteers paid an honorarium, not as employees. This demand, rising at the same time from Karnataka to Uttarakhand, shows that the model of cheaply squeezing women's labour without a pension or social security can no longer last.
sawal: What will an ASHA who cared for a village's health for years get in her old age?
ref: ASHA
Accredited Social Health Activists, who have worked in villages since 2005 under the National Rural Health Mission. They get no salary, only an honorarium and incentives based on the work done.
ask: A five lakh rupee retirement package and a pension

h: UAPA charges against Rejaz Siddique dropped after 560 days in jail
dek: A Nagpur sessions court has discharged the Kerala journalist from UAPA charges, but he will be tried under other sections and has not yet got bail.
body: The district and sessions court in Nagpur has discharged Kerala journalist and student activist Rejaz M. Sheeba Siddique from charges under the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, or UAPA. The court has now ordered charges to be framed under Sections 152 and 353(1) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita. Section 152 deals with endangering the sovereignty, unity and integrity of the country and was brought in to replace the old sedition law.

Rejaz was arrested in Nagpur on 7 May 2025 over alleged links with banned organisations. A week later the Maharashtra ATS took over the investigation and added Sections 38 and 39 of UAPA. The investigating agency had cited as evidence Signal and Telegram chats, some phone numbers, literature on the CPI (Maoist), Kashmir and armed groups, and photos taken at a gun shop.

Rejaz, who was 26 at the time of his arrest, studied social work at the University of Kerala and has written on police excesses, discrimination and prison conditions for platforms like Maktoob and Countercurrents. He has been in Nagpur Central Jail for 560 days and several of his bail pleas have been rejected. The next bail hearing is on 3 December.
nazar: After more than a year and a half in jail, the court did not find the UAPA charges holding up. That is the strongest comment on how this law is used. Keeping books and writing were turned into proof of terror, and the punishment was served before the trial. That this happened to a young Muslim journalist who wrote on police excesses and prisoners is a frightening message for other independent journalists too.
sawal: Who will answer for 560 days in jail?
ref: Sections 38 and 39 of UAPA
Sections on membership of a terrorist organisation (38) and giving it support (39). Getting bail in UAPA cases is extremely hard.

h: Rampur's metalsmiths: our skill, the trader's name
dek: In Rampur, Uttar Pradesh, artisans who work copper and brass are keeping their inherited craft alive amid rising metal prices, toxic fumes and namelessness.
body: Eighty-year-old Mohammad Sharif has been beating metal since the age of twelve and has taught the craft to many people in Rampur, some of whom are exporters today. Now his sons Shahzade Alam and Mohammad Shadab Ali make pitchers, paan boxes, utensils, vases and, most of all, copper wall plates in a one-room workshop near a mosque. Rampur's craft is linked to the brass tradition of Moradabad, an hour away, which got a GI tag in 2014.

The work runs on orders from traders in Delhi or Moradabad. First a sample is made, then half the money is taken in advance to buy raw material. A 15 kg copper sheet costs 12,000 to 15,000 rupees and makes about 18 plates. After the sheet is cut, the design is traced on with tracing paper and engraved with hammer and chisel, an iron rod is fitted to the edges, and 'dhalai', done with small stamps, makes the piece sturdy.

Polishing comes last, either 'nikhar' with acid or 'qalai' with tin. Mohammad Guddu, who does qalai, explains that keeping food in copper without a coating is not safe. Tin is melted onto a vessel heated in a furnace, but the fumes cause breathing illness. Guddu's father did the same work and died of TB. He says that even if he quit, he would not get a job outside paying more than ten thousand.

A plate sells for a thousand to twelve hundred rupees, with five hundred extra for polishing. When copper became costlier, the artisans cut their own wages, fearing they would lose orders if they bargained too hard. Shahzade earns 18,000 to 25,000 a month and Shadab 15,000 to 18,000, with no fixed income. Mohammad Parvez, 52, hired to help, gets five hundred rupees a day, and on other days drives a rented e-rickshaw.

Mohammad Suhail, who runs his own workshop in the utensils market, is an expert at making pitchers. He says workshops were once so big that ten people sat together, and now low wages have taken the life out of the work. The biggest complaint is about recognition: traders sell the goods under their own brand, and the maker's name appears nowhere. Sameer Alam, who wrote this report, died in October 2026.
nazar: This story from Rampur is a glimpse of a larger system in which the skill of Muslim artisans sells in the market, but the profit and the name go to middlemen. Schemes like the GI tag and 'One District One Product' are hollow until the artisan gets a fair price, protection for his health and the right to his name on his work.
sawal: Whose responsibility is the treatment of an artisan made ill by qalai fumes?
ref: GI tag

Geographical Indication, a legal identity for a special product linked to a region.
Moradabad's brass work got it in 2014.
Qalai

The work of coating copper and brass vessels with a layer of tin.
It keeps the vessel from turning black and makes it fit to hold food.

h: Villages that make goldsmiths' dies, in the shadow of Vadhavan port
dek: In villages along Dahanu creek in Palghar, a sixty-year-old trade in moulds for gold jewellery fears floods and displacement from Vadhavan port.
body: In eight or nine villages around Dahanu creek in Maharashtra's Palghar district, thousands of artisans make 'dies', or moulds, for gold jewellery. There is no official count of them. The grandfather of 35-year-old Santosh Raut of Tighare Pada learnt the work in Chinchani Tarapur in the sixties and bought a hand drill with his own and his relatives' money. The trade is also mentioned in a 1981 government handicrafts survey.

According to Santosh, every pair of hands here has work. Customers come on their own from Madhya Pradesh, Rajasthan and Bihar, and from as far as Nepal, Dubai, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh. Santosh, who studied up to Class 10, bought a CNC machine worth eight lakh rupees with his savings four years ago. In the monsoon, when the fish catch is low, fishermen also work here as helpers. He says that if you can earn in the village itself, who would go to the city?

Vadhavan port is being built in this same creek. It is a partnership of the Jawaharlal Nehru Port Authority and the Maharashtra Maritime Board and part of the Sagarmala programme. The project spreads over 17,471 hectares of tidal area. The government claims it will create a million jobs, and Chief Minister Fadnavis calls it the economic engine for the next thirty years.

The environmental impact assessment says no village will be moved, so there is no human cost. The artisans ask where the water will go when 1,448 hectares of sea are filled in and a 10.14 km breakwater is built. Marine researcher Prof. Bhushan Bhoir says this could change the balance of silt and erosion on the coast and increase monsoon flooding.

The die makers are not on the 'project affected' list, because their land was not acquired. The socio-economic assessment mentions them in just one line. Villagers fear that one day floods, erosion or salt water will force them to leave their homes and work without compensation. Farmers, fishermen and artisans have been protesting for about two months, just as they did when the project was first proposed in the nineties.
nazar: The accounting of development is incomplete when it counts only land papers and leaves out the people whose livelihood rests on water, the coast and the shape of the village. The question at Vadhavan is whether a self-reliant rural economy must first be destroyed before it is counted as a 'loss'.
sawal: If the land was not taken, is there no compensation even when the livelihood goes?
ref: Vadhavan port

A large container port being built at Dahanu in Palghar, on an artificial island in the sea.
Local fishermen and villages have opposed it since the 1990s.
Project Affected Person (PAP)

People the government considers affected by a project and entitled to compensation and rehabilitation.
The list usually rests on land acquisition.

h: The weight of Punjab's 'green energy' falls on Dalit workers
dek: This PARI film shows landless Dalit and OBC workers in Sangrur who load bundles of 40 to 50 kg of paddy husk, burnt in place of coal, into trolleys.
body: This short film comes with the PARI report 'Carrying the load of green energy', recorded by researcher Gaurav Bansal in Sangrur district in Punjab's Malwa region. Its subject is paddy husk, which is now burnt in kilns and factories in place of coal, and the workers who carry it.

On a foggy winter morning, in the dark, eleven men climb into a truck, most of them from landless Dalit and OBC families, some of them educated. They often do not know whether they will travel forty kilometres today or a hundred. All day they load husk (phoos or chhilka in Punjabi) and wheat straw into big trolleys, called 'bhung' there. These trolleys go to Punjab, Haryana, Himachal, Delhi NCR and Rajasthan.

The method is simple and heavy. Two men place a 40 to 50 kg bundle on a co-worker's head, he climbs a ladder of about twenty feet and tips it into the trolley, and men standing on top press it down with their feet to make room. Each man carries hundreds of bundles a day. An eight or nine hour day stretches to fourteen hours. A gang of ten or twelve gets 22 rupees a quintal, which means six or seven hundred rupees in each man's hand.

The workers say this is better than bonded-like service as a 'siri' for a landlord, because here they work for one another. In Malwa it is among the best paid casual jobs. But where a truck once held 120 to 125 quintals, it now holds 300 to 350 quintals, while wages have barely risen. The palledar (loaders') union has broken up, and there is no way to bargain.

Husk was once waste, thrown outside sheller mills. Upheavals in coal and a government rule requiring 20 per cent biomass to be mixed in turned it into a valuable fuel, and the benefit went to brokers, traders and mill owners. Sunam block alone has about ninety rice mills.

The workers' bodies pay the price. Knees give way by forty, and back pain and breathing trouble from hot, prickly dust are common. The nearest working health centre is seven kilometres away, so quacks do the treating. Addiction to tramadol is spreading as a way to fight exhaustion. One worker has been bedridden since a trolley accident in 2021, and a small sum from the broker was his only protection. The names of workers and villages in the report have been changed.
nazar: In the debate on 'green energy', carbon is counted, but not the backs this fuel is carried on. If the energy transition only repeats the old ladder of caste, with the profit going to the mill owner and the burden to the landless Dalit, it cannot be called just. Along with the biomass rule there should be a rule on these workers' wages, insurance and health.
sawal: Who set 22 rupees a quintal for a 300 quintal trolley?
ref: Co-firing

Burning a share of biomass (husk, stubble and so on) along with coal.
In Punjab, kilns and industries must use at least 20 per cent.
Siri

A farm labourer in Punjab bound to a landlord for a year.
Often because of debt, he is forced to work whenever called.

h: Nityanand Tiwari's criticism: history, modernity and the test of plot
dek: Vinod Tiwari reads the critical vision of Nityanand Tiwari, the critic who died this week, as standing on two pillars: a sense of history and modernity.
body: Vinod Tiwari, who teaches in the Hindi department of Delhi University, was not formally a student of Nityanand Tiwari, yet he regards him as his guru. He says it was from Nityanand ji that he learnt how medieval literature should be read and what plot really is. The essay is taken from the journal 'Samkaleen Soch' and was published on Sammukh after the critic's death.

The writer argues that Nityanand Tiwari's criticism rests on two foundations, history and modernity. His sense of history teaches him to read a work within its society and culture. He returns again and again to Lukacs's idea of the 'historical individual' and asks how far a work stands up to that test. Three words, form, perception and making (vidhan, bodh and nirmiti), run through all his writing.

His debate on writing the history of literature is especially important. Ramchandra Shukla identified a period by one dominant 'lok-pravritti' (popular tendency), while Hazariprasad Dwivedi said an age is made by the relations among many tendencies, which run sometimes straight, sometimes slanting and sometimes in conflict. Nityanand Tiwari takes this debate further and adopts Muktibodh's method, which looks at a work's social source, its inner form and its effect, all three.

The writer sees him as a widely read Marxist who did not accept literature empty of ideology, because in his view such literature often leans towards the status quo. 'Padmavat' is at the centre of his historical framework, but he also did serious work on Nayi Kavita (new poetry), Akavita (anti-poetry), the novel and drama.

A large part of the essay is about his idea of 'plot'. For him, plot is not just a string of events, it has roots in historical and social reality. He credits Premchand with giving the Hindi novel its plot, and sees 'Maila Anchal' (The Soiled Border) as a novel that breaks Premchand's framework and still opens new possibilities for plot.
nazar: At a time when uncomfortable writers are being removed from university syllabi, Nityanand Tiwari's insistence that literature cannot be read cut off from its society and history is worth remembering. To hold Premchand and Renu to the test of plot is really to put the village, the farmer and life on the margins at the centre of literature.
sawal: Is 'Maila Anchal' taught with this depth in today's classrooms?
ref: Nityanand Tiwari
Marxist Hindi critic and professor at Delhi University. His work on medieval and modern literature is considered important.
Lok-pravritti
Ramchandra Shukla's idea that every literary period is identified by one main popular tendency of its time.

h: A student's farewell to the teacher who taught 'Pralay ki Chhaya'
dek: Garima Srivastava remembers her research guide Nityanand Tiwari through the classroom, Skype calls and memories of Santiniketan.
body: This memoir by Garima Srivastava, professor at the Centre of Indian Languages in JNU, is for her research guide Nityanand Tiwari, who died this week at the age of 88. According to her, his real legacy lives in his students as well as his books.

It begins in an MA class at the Arts Faculty, where he was teaching Jaishankar Prasad's poem 'Pralay ki Chhaya' (The Shadow of Doom). He told the students not to weigh the poem against the facts of history, and then read it in a slow, deep voice. The writer recalls that even after tiring rides in DTC buses, the rhythm of that class stayed with her for a long time.

The memoir then moves to Europe, where the writer was going through a period of loneliness and mental strain. In conversations on Skype, Tiwari ji asked her to send her handwritten diaries and told her not to tear them up. According to her, he also showed those pages to Vishwanath Tripathi and encouraged her to publish them.

There are also memories of Santiniketan's Poush Mela, Baul songs and the cotton dhotis bought for him. His speech on Premchand's novels at a seminar in Hyderabad became the basis of her essay on 'Sevasadan', which he later praised.

After Covid his health and memory began to fail. The writer says he had started calling himself a dried-up pond and would promise to call as soon as his strength returned. The memoir ends with a poem by Nirala, on the thought that even in old age, the memories of life stay green.
nazar: This memoir is a reminder of how great a support a good teacher in a public university is for women students from different backgrounds who travel in by bus. As pressure grows on the fees, funding and freedom of these institutions, the value of such relationships becomes clearer.
sawal: How many teachers today advise a student not to tear up her diaries?
ref: Pralay ki Chhaya
A long poem by Jaishankar Prasad that holds history and emotion together through the inner struggle of Queen Kamala of Gujarat.
Poush Mela
A fair held every year in Santiniketan in the month of Poush, known for Baul singers and folk crafts.

h: Reading Fanon in Mumbai's bastis
dek: Amit Kumar reads the Hindi translation of 'A Dying Colonialism' in the light of bulldozers in slums, Dharavi and the scrutiny of voter lists.
body: The review begins in Mumbai. According to the writer, in September 2026 the Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation announced action against about 39,000 unauthorised structures taller than 14 feet in slum settlements. The reason given was building safety, but residents asked where families who had lived there for years would go. The drive was halted after protests. Amit Kumar calls this the basic contradiction of the modern city: the people who keep the city running are not given the right to live in it.

Against this he places 'Samrajyavad ka Bujhta Diya', the Hindi translation of Frantz Fanon's 1959 book on Algeria's freedom struggle. Fanon's core argument is that domination works not only through police and law but also through everyday relationships, culture and self-image. The chapters on medicine and radio show that distrust of colonial technology came from history, not ignorance, and that the same radio later became a weapon of the struggle.

The writer brings together Lefebvre's 'right to the city', David Harvey and Partha Chatterjee's idea of 'political society' to arrive at the gap between legal and social legitimacy. In Dharavi, according to him, about 24,000 families received notices in March 2026 to submit papers. The question is whether the lack of papers is always proof that someone did not live there.

He raises the same question about the Special Intensive Revision of electoral rolls, which was protested in October, and carries it to the demand for statehood for Jammu and Kashmir. On caste, he places Ambedkar and Fanon side by side: can formal freedom be complete in an unequal social structure?

The review also lists Fanon's limits, for instance that although women's role grew during the war, equality did not come in free Algeria. The translation is by Akshat Jain and Shahadat, made from English rather than French, and the writer also questions the choice of 'samrajyavad' (imperialism) over 'upniveshvad' (colonialism) in the title.
nazar: This review takes the book out of the library and straight into the basti. The practice of deciding citizenship and residence by papers, which is spreading from slums to voter lists, hits migrant workers, Dalits, Muslims and women the hardest, since they often have the fewest papers.
sawal: Where will the memories of Dharavi homes that have no papers be recorded?
ref: Frantz Fanon
Psychiatrist and thinker born in Martinique, who took part in Algeria's freedom struggle and wrote on the psychological roots of colonialism.
Political society
Partha Chatterjee's idea that the urban poor bargain with the state collectively as communities rather than as individual citizens.

h: 'Pyre': emptying hills, a shepherd and burning pyres
dek: Saurabh Anant does not review Vinod Kapri's film 'Pyre', he records in prose the feeling it leaves behind.
body: The writer says plainly that this is not a film review but an account of the feelings that stayed inside after watching Vinod Kapri's film 'Pyre'. So the piece opens up the world of the film in images more than it tells the story: the mountains, the empty villages and the absence of people.

At its centre is an old shepherd who leaves home with his sick wife to get her treated, and takes a goat along, the way old people once carried money on a journey. On the way back, the goat's absence fills the silence between them. Along the road, smoke from pyres burning on the riverbank can be seen.

The writer turns the mountain paths into a metaphor for waiting. A path that was watched for over the years slowly grows over with grass and melts back into the mountain. The people who went down from the village never came back. Their mud houses melt in the rain and wash down the slopes, and for those left behind only strange letters come up from below.

The goats are lost one by one. In the end the shepherd climbs to the mountain top and blows a horn, and builds a pyre for his wife. To the writer, in the crumbling village these pyres seem like the mountains' last creation.
The writer says Kapri has recorded a world whose silence speaks very loudly. The film keeps playing in the mind after it ends, and he appeals to readers not just to watch it but to feel it.
nazar: The 'ghost villages' of Uttarakhand and Himachal are not a poetic fancy but the direct result of having no jobs, roads or hospitals. The old couple setting out to sell a goat for treatment is the face of a mountain reality that never shows up in tourism ads.
sawal: Which hospital would the shepherd taking a goat for his wife's treatment have reached?
ref: Vinod Kapri
A journalist turned film director whose films often focus on the struggles of ordinary people and on migration.
Palayan
The large-scale movement of people from Uttarakhand's hill villages to towns below in search of jobs and facilities, which has left many villages almost deserted.

h: Chhath without Sharda Sinha, yet her voice is on the ghat
dek: Musharraf Parvez writes on Chhath songs, the festival's market, and the pull of Sharda Sinha's voice that takes people far from home back to their village ghat.
body: Musharraf Parvez makes it clear at the start that his essay is not about the religious side of Chhath but about its songs. He is speaking to readers who love the sun, the river, the ghat and the smell of riverbank earth.

He describes Chhath as a festival of folk faith that runs for four days from Kartik Shukla Shashthi, in which people stand in water and offer arghya to the setting and rising sun. According to the writer, what makes it special is that it needs no priest, and men fast as well as women.

The essay also pauses on the Chhath market. Spades for building ghats, bamboo baskets, sugarcane, radish, bananas and coconuts all sell fast in these days. The writer sees it as a yearly fair whose benefits reach small artisans and small farmers.

Then the talk turns to Sharda Sinha, whose Maithili and Bhojpuri songs made her the voice of Bihar. The writer says that as soon as Diwali is over, people settled across the country and abroad start listening to her Chhath songs, and these songs pull them back to their village ghat. According to him, Sharda Sinha sang more than sixty Chhath songs.
The last part of the essay says the artist goes but the art remains. Sharda Sinha is no more, but as long as Chhath is celebrated, her voice will echo on the ghats.
nazar: A large part of the power of Chhath songs is the story of migration from Bihar: workers in Delhi, Surat and the Gulf look for home in these songs. And this essay, written by a Muslim writer on the folk tradition of Chhath, is a reminder that this shared culture is not the property of any one community.
sawal: Which song do workers who cannot go home for Chhath listen to?
ref: Sharda Sinha
Folk singer from Bihar whose Maithili and Bhojpuri Chhath songs have been the sound of the festival for generations.
Arghya
The Chhath ritual of standing in a river or pond and offering water and prasad to the setting and rising sun.

h: A Davangere childhood: poverty, the akhada and a weeping mother
dek: This extract from Kannada writer Vijaya's autobiography recalls a childhood of poverty, a house full of men and small joys in a town of the princely state of Mysore.
body: Scroll has published an extract from 'After the Fire', the English translation of Kannada writer Vijaya's autobiography. The translation is by Krishna Manavalli and the book is from Speaking Tiger. This part is about the writer's childhood in Davangere, which was then part of the princely state of Mysore.

In the government school the king's song was sung instead of a prayer, and on the king's birthday sugar and sweets were handed out from bullock carts. According to the writer, people took this with affection, not fear, and this reverence lasted for some time even after Independence. She also remembers a freedom fighter who threw a slipper at the royal palanquin and went to jail.

Outside the school an old woman sold ber (jujube), jaggery and coconut sweets and oranges stuffed with spices. The children stole a little money and tamarind and jaggery from home to buy them. Davangere was famous for wrestling, and little Vijaya went to the akhada on the pretext of feeding the pigeons and learnt the wrestlers' moves. One day a new boy threw her down and teased her as a Brahmin girl. She answered back, but then stopped going to the akhada.

At home her grandmother cursed her mother at every turn, saying she did not look after the children and had too many of them. Her mother beat Vijaya badly and then secretly fed her sweets and told her not to tell anyone. Linking an uncle's death to an inauspicious hour, the family moved to a dark house with no electricity, and according to the writer it was in this period that her schooling stopped, and no one even noticed.

Her mother, struggling with asthma, painted the walls of the house with a cloth brush and the juice of tomato leaves, yet her grandmother kept calling her lazy. The extract ends on an unresolved memory: letters found in the attic, after reading which her mother cried for three days and did not eat.
nazar: A girl's schooling stops and 'no one even noticed': that line is still the story of lakhs of homes today. Vijaya's memoir shows that even an upper caste home in poverty can be just as suffocating for women, where a mother's illness is taken for laziness and a daughter's education for something useless.
sawal: What was in those letters in the attic that made her mother cry for three days?
ref: Vijaya
Senior Kannada writer, journalist and film critic. The English translation of her autobiography has been published as 'After the Fire'.
Garadi
In Karnataka the traditional wrestling akhada is called a garadi, where wrestlers train.
